The remarkable CNN exchange that took the Ted Cruz affair rumors from the tabloids into the mainstream.

This article is bizarre.

The disheartening reality for journalists is that the Republican presidential front-runner and his allies are getting frighteningly good at forcing them down roads they have tried to avoid.

Just stop for a minute and think of how warped that is. We now live in a world where a "journalist" will actually complain about someone forcing journalists to stop avoiding a story.

Honestly, after reading the the National Enquirer article, I see no supporting evidence. All I see from the Enquirer is the pushing of little more than rumors. And rumors should not be the basis of journalism. It might be the start of a journalistic investigation. But you don't report on it unless you have evidence.

And rumors should not be the basis of journalism.

Yes and no.

Rumors arguably should not be a basis for reporting that a thing happened, since they aren't sufficient evidence that it happened. However, it should be noted that they very often ARE explicitly a basis for reporting that a thing happened. If one wishes to be precise about it, every single news article that quotes unnamed sources as saying that this or that happened is reporting "rumors." It's more complex than all that though, and I'll come back to that later.

In any event, even setting aside that issue, the rumors themselves are potentially newsworthy. It can be, and arguably should be, reported that the rumors exist, simply because the rumors do in fact exist.

It might be the start of a journalistic investigation.

It not only might be, but should be.

But you don't report on it unless you have evidence.

And to go back to my first sentence, journalists regularly report on things for which they don't have hard evidence. That is, in fact, a considerable part of all reporting. It's acceptable because they aren't actually reporting that <thus and such> happened - they're reporting that "according to <source>, <thus and such> happened." So by the strictest interpretation, they aren't in fact reporting that a thing happened - they're reporting that a source said that a thing happened. It's a subtle distinction, but one that must be understood in order to really understand how journalism works.

And the fact remains that at no point did the author of this article even hint at further investigation or unsubstantiated claims or any of that. Instead, he forthrightly took the position that it was a story that they were "trying to avoid," and he decried the fact that the Trump campaign made it such that they could no longer continue to do that.

However, it should be noted that they very often ARE explicitly a basis for reporting that a thing happened.
